item.title: Linear algebra 1: same arrow, new recipe
item.description:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.

The numbers are a recipe

What is (6, 4)? Two numbers.
Is it an arrow? Not yet. It’s what we write down for one.
What do the numbers say? Walk 6 steps along one arrow, then 4 along another.
What are those two arrows called? The basis. Think of them as ingredients.
And (6, 4)? The recipe: how much of each ingredient.

On the right, what are the ingredients? c₁, one step right, and c₂, one step up.
What is the recipe for x? (6, 4).
On the left, what are the ingredients? b₁ = (4, 1) and b₂ = (−6, 1).
What is the recipe for x? (3, 1). Three of b₁ goes far right; one of b₂ comes back.
Two pictures, two recipes. How many arrows? One. The arrow didn’t move.
Then what changed? The ingredients, and so the recipe.

The recipe is a picture. Here are the official words, the ones Lay uses (4.4) [Lay16]:

  • b₁ and b₂ are the basis vectors of a basis, called B;
  • the recipe (3, 1) is the coordinates of x relative to B, written ;
  • c₁ and c₂, the usual grid, are the standard basis.

From here on, we use those words.

Drag the tips of b₁ and b₂. The black arrow x stays where it is.

x = [6, 4]
B1 = "#7570b3"   // b₁ and everything made of it (purple)
B2 = "#d95f02"   // b₂ and everything made of it (orange)

viewof basis = {
  const X0 = -8, X1 = 14, Y0 = -4, Y1 = 9, S = 26;      // S px per unit
  const W = (X1 - X0) * S, H = (Y1 - Y0) * S;
  const px = p => [(p[0] - X0) * S, (Y1 - p[1]) * S];
  const fromPx = (u, v) => [Math.round(u / S + X0), Math.round(Y1 - v / S)];
  const state = {b1: [4, 1], b2: [-6, 1]};
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", `${W}px`)
    .style("touch-action", "none");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  for (const [id, color] of [["t1", B1], ["t2", B2], ["tk", "black"]])
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 9).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5)
      .attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10z").attr("fill", color);
  const g = svg.append("g");
  const node = svg.node();

  function arrow(p, q, color, width, tip, opacity = 1) {
    const [a, b] = [px(p), px(q)];
    g.append("line").attr("x1", a[0]).attr("y1", a[1]).attr("x2", b[0])
      .attr("y2", b[1]).attr("stroke", color).attr("stroke-width", width)
      .attr("stroke-opacity", opacity)
      .attr("marker-end", tip ? `url(#${tip})` : null);
  }
  function label(p, text, color) {
    const [a, b] = px(p);
    g.append("text").attr("x", a[0] + 10).attr("y", b - 10)
      .attr("fill", color).attr("font-size", 17).text(text);
  }
  function draw() {
    g.selectAll("*").remove();
    const {b1, b2} = state;
    const det = b1[0] * b2[1] - b2[0] * b1[1];
    if (det !== 0) {                    // the grid the ingredients make
      for (let k = -40; k <= 40; k++)
        for (const [d, o] of [[b1, b2], [b2, b1]])
          arrow([k * o[0] - 60 * d[0], k * o[1] - 60 * d[1]],
                [k * o[0] + 60 * d[0], k * o[1] + 60 * d[1]],
                "#999", 0.7, null, 0.3);
      const r1 = (x[0] * b2[1] - b2[0] * x[1]) / det;  // walk the recipe:
      const mid = [r1 * b1[0], r1 * b1[1]];            // so much b₁,
      arrow([0, 0], mid, B1, 2.5, "t1", 0.6);
      arrow(mid, x, B2, 2.5, "t2", 0.6);               // then b₂
    }
    arrow([0, 0], x, "black", 3.5, "tk");
    arrow([0, 0], b1, B1, 5, "t1");
    arrow([0, 0], b2, B2, 5, "t2");
    for (const [p, name, color] of [[b1, "b₁", B1], [b2, "b₂", B2]]) {
      const [a, b] = px(p);
      g.append("circle").attr("cx", a[0]).attr("cy", b).attr("r", 9)
        .attr("fill", color).attr("fill-opacity", 0.3)
        .style("cursor", "grab");
      label(p, name, color);
    }
    label(x, "x", "black");
    node.value = {b1: [...b1], b2: [...b2]};
    node.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  }

  let dragging = null;
  const local = e => {
    const r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
    return [(e.clientX - r.left) * W / r.width, (e.clientY - r.top) * H / r.height];
  };
  node.addEventListener("pointerdown", e => {
    const [u, v] = local(e);
    const dist = k => Math.hypot(px(state[k])[0] - u, px(state[k])[1] - v);
    const k = dist("b1") < dist("b2") ? "b1" : "b2";
    if (dist(k) < 24) { dragging = k; node.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointermove", e => {
    if (!dragging) return;
    const p = fromPx(...local(e));
    if (p[0] === 0 && p[1] === 0) return;           // no zero ingredient
    if (p[0] !== state[dragging][0] || p[1] !== state[dragging][1]) {
      state[dragging] = p; draw();
    }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointerup", () => { dragging = null; });
  draw();
  return node;
}
// The recipe, written with each ingredient as a column in its colour:
//   x = r1·(b1) + r2·(b2)
// Part 1's dictionary section points back here: these columns are P.
{
  const {b1, b2} = basis;
  const det = b1[0] * b2[1] - b2[0] * b1[1];
  if (det === 0) return md`b₁ and b₂ lie along one line.
No mix of them reaches x.`;
  const r1 = (x[0] * b2[1] - b2[0] * x[1]) / det;
  const r2 = (b1[0] * x[1] - x[0] * b1[1]) / det;
  const f = n => Number.isInteger(n) ? `${n}` : n.toFixed(2);
  const col = (v, color) => html`<span style="display:inline-flex;
    flex-direction:column; align-items:flex-end; vertical-align:middle;
    border-left:2px solid ${color}; border-right:2px solid ${color};
    border-radius:.8em; padding:0 .45em; margin:0 .2em; color:${color}; font-weight:600">
    <span>${f(v[0])}</span><span>${f(v[1])}</span></span>`;
  const sum = [r1 * b1[0] + r2 * b2[0], r1 * b1[1] + r2 * b2[1]];
  return html`<div style="font-size:1.3em; font-family:monospace">
    x = <span style="color:${B1}">${f(r1)}</span>·${col(b1, B1)}
    + <span style="color:${B2}">${f(r2)}</span>·${col(b2, B2)}
    = ${col(sum, "black")}</div>
    <p>The coordinates of x in this basis are
    (<span style="color:${B1}">${f(r1)}</span>,
     <span style="color:${B2}">${f(r2)}</span>).</p>`;
}
Put b₁ back at (4, 1) and drag only b₂. Does x’s amount of b₁ change? Yes, though b₁ never moved. Odd. Part 3 explains it.
NoteThe Law of Coordinates

A vector’s numbers are its coordinates in some basis. Change the basis, and the coordinates change. The arrow does not.

The dictionary

You’ve been dragging b₁ and b₂ wherever you like. Now let’s fix one example and work it by hand. If you moved them, put them back where they started:

  • the old basis B is b₁ = (4, 1) and b₂ = (−6, 1);
  • the new basis C is the usual grid, c₁ one step right and c₂ one step up;
  • the arrow is x, whose coordinates in B are .

The question: what are x’s coordinates in C, ?

How do we turn into without drawing? Look up each basis vector of B in c-words, like words in a dictionary.
What is b₁, in c-words? 4c₁ + c₂, or the column (4, 1).
And b₂? −6c₁ + c₂, or the column (−6, 1).
So what is 3b₁ + b₂? 3(4c₁ + c₂) + (−6c₁ + c₂) = 6c₁ + 4c₂. Coordinates (6, 4).
Where is the matrix? Push the two columns together.

Column 1 is b₁; column 2 is b₂.

What is P(3, 1)? 3 of column 1, plus 1 of column 2: (6, 4).
Where have we seen that? In the coloured line under the drag picture. Drag b₁, and column 1 changes with it.
So what is P? A dictionary. Each column is one basis vector of B, looked up in C: and .
What does Lay call it? The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C, , with (4.7).
NoteThe Law of Change of Coordinates

To change coordinates from B to C, write each vector of B in C’s coordinates. Those are the columns of .

A friend writes with its columns as rows: . What do they get for (3, 1)? (13, −17).
Is that x? No. x is (6, 4).
What went wrong? Each row mixes parts of b₁ and b₂. A column holds one whole basis vector.

To check your understanding, here is Lay’s 4.4, Example 1. The basis is b₁ = (1, 0) and b₂ = (1, 2), and . What is x? Decide before you read on.

What is −2·b₁ + 3·b₂? −2·(1, 0) + 3·(1, 2) = (1, 6).

Why anyone bothers

Where does A send (1, 0)? To (2, 1). Stretched and turned.
Where does A send (1, 1)? To (3, 3).
Turned? No. Same direction, three times as long.
And (−1, 1)? To (−1, 1). It doesn’t move at all.

Along (1, 1) and (−1, 1), what does A do? Only stretches: by 3, and by 1.
If those were our basis, what would A do to coordinates? Multiply the first by 3 and leave the second alone: the matrix (3 0; 0 1). Same A, new matrix, as simple as a matrix gets.
How do we find such a basis? That is part 2.

In Lay

Here Lay
ingredients b₁, b₂ basis vectors of a basis B (4.3)
recipe (3, 1) coordinates of x relative to B, (4.4)
the usual grid the standard basis (4.4)
the dictionary P change-of-coordinates matrix (4.7); when C is standard (4.4)
our worked example 4.7, Example 1

References

[Lay16] D. C. Lay, S. R. Lay, J. J. McDonald, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 5th ed., Pearson, 2016. The Math 54 text at UC Berkeley. Section and example numbers in this series follow this edition. This series is not affiliated with UC Berkeley or the publisher.

item.title: Linear algebra 2: the basis where it only stretches
item.description:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.

Part 1 ended with a matrix that turns most arrows but leaves two directions alone:

This part uses those two directions as the basis.

Arrows that don’t turn

Drag the tip of v. The orange arrow is Av, where A sends it.

A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]
apply = (M, p) => [M[0][0] * p[0] + M[0][1] * p[1],
                   M[1][0] * p[0] + M[1][1] * p[1]]

viewof v = {
  const X0 = -7, X1 = 7, Y0 = -7, Y1 = 7, S = 26;       // S px per unit
  const W = (X1 - X0) * S, H = (Y1 - Y0) * S;
  const px = p => [(p[0] - X0) * S, (Y1 - p[1]) * S];
  const fromPx = (u, w) => [Math.round(u / S + X0), Math.round(Y1 - w / S)];
  let state = [1, 0];
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", `${W}px`)
    .style("touch-action", "none");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  for (const [id, color] of [["v2t1", "#7570b3"], ["v2t2", "#d95f02"]])
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 9).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5)
      .attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10z").attr("fill", color);
  const g = svg.append("g");
  const node = svg.node();
  function arrow(p, q, color, width, tip, opacity = 1) {
    const [a, b] = [px(p), px(q)];
    g.append("line").attr("x1", a[0]).attr("y1", a[1]).attr("x2", b[0])
      .attr("y2", b[1]).attr("stroke", color).attr("stroke-width", width)
      .attr("stroke-opacity", opacity)
      .attr("marker-end", tip ? `url(#${tip})` : null);
  }
  function draw() {
    g.selectAll("*").remove();
    for (let k = X0; k <= X1; k++) {                    // plain grid
      arrow([k, Y0], [k, Y1], "#999", 0.7, null, 0.25);
      arrow([X0, k], [X1, k], "#999", 0.7, null, 0.25);
    }
    const Av = apply(A, state);
    const own = state[0] * Av[1] - state[1] * Av[0] === 0;
    if (own)                                            // its own line
      arrow([-20 * state[0], -20 * state[1]], [20 * state[0], 20 * state[1]],
            "#7570b3", 2, null, 0.35);
    arrow([0, 0], Av, "#d95f02", 4, "v2t2");
    arrow([0, 0], state, "#7570b3", 5, "v2t1");
    const [a, b] = px(state);
    g.append("circle").attr("cx", a).attr("cy", b).attr("r", 9)
      .attr("fill", "#7570b3").attr("fill-opacity", 0.3)
      .style("cursor", "grab");
    g.append("text").attr("x", a + 10).attr("y", b - 10)
      .attr("fill", "#7570b3").attr("font-size", 17).text("v");
    const [c, d] = px(Av);
    g.append("text").attr("x", c + 10).attr("y", d - 10)
      .attr("fill", "#d95f02").attr("font-size", 17).text("Av");
    node.value = [...state];
    node.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  }
  let dragging = false;
  const local = e => {
    const r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
    return [(e.clientX - r.left) * W / r.width, (e.clientY - r.top) * H / r.height];
  };
  node.addEventListener("pointerdown", e => {
    const [u, w] = local(e);
    const [a, b] = px(state);
    if (Math.hypot(a - u, b - w) < 24) {
      dragging = true; node.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
    }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointermove", e => {
    if (!dragging) return;
    const p = fromPx(...local(e));
    if (p[0] === 0 && p[1] === 0) return;
    if (Math.abs(p[0]) > 3 || Math.abs(p[1]) > 3) return; // keep Av on screen
    if (p[0] !== state[0] || p[1] !== state[1]) { state = p; draw(); }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointerup", () => { dragging = false; });
  draw();
  return node;
}
{
  const Av = apply(A, v);
  const own = v[0] * Av[1] - v[1] * Av[0] === 0;
  const k = (Av[0] * v[0] + Av[1] * v[1]) / (v[0] * v[0] + v[1] * v[1]);
  return html`<div style="font-size:1.2em; font-family:monospace">
    v = (${v[0]}, ${v[1]})  →  Av = (${Av[0]}, ${Av[1]})</div>
    <p>${own
      ? html`<b>Av = ${k}·v.</b> A doesn't turn this arrow; it only stretches it, by ${k}.`
      : "A turned this arrow."}</p>`;
}
Drag v around. Does Av usually point the same way as v? No. A turns most arrows.
Which arrows does it not turn? Those along (1, 1), and those along (−1, 1).
What does it do to them? Stretches them: by 3 along (1, 1), by 1 along (−1, 1).
What are they called? Eigenvectors. Eigen is German for “own”: each is A’s own arrow, keeping to its own line. Think “own arrow”.
And the 3 and the 1? Eigenvalues: how much each one stretches.

To check your understanding, here is the matrix Lay opens 5.1 with (Example 1):

Where does it send v = (2, 1)? To (4, 2) = 2v. An eigenvector, with eigenvalue 2. Lay’s words: it only “stretches” v.
And u = (−1, 1)? To (−5, −1). Turned: not an eigenvector.

What does A do to x?

Call the two eigenvectors v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1), and take one arrow to work with, x = (2, 0): its coordinates in the standard basis.

Where does A send x? We could multiply A by x. Instead we’ll take three easy steps.

Step 1. Translate x into v’s.

What are x’s coordinates in v’s? (1, −1), because 1·v₁ − 1·v₂ = (1, 1) − (−1, 1) = (2, 0).

Step 2. Stretch.

What does A do to v₁? Stretches it by 3.
And to v₂? Leaves it as it is: a stretch by 1.
So what are Ax’s coordinates in v’s? (3·1, 1·(−1)) = (3, −1).

Step 3. Translate back into the usual grid.

What is (3, −1) in v’s, in the usual grid? 3·v₁ − 1·v₂ = (3, 3) − (−1, 1) = (4, 2).
Check the long way: what is A(2, 0)? (2·2 + 1·0, 1·2 + 2·0) = (4, 2). The same.

Naming the steps

We did the three steps with numbers. Each one is also a matrix. Name them, and A fits on one line.

Step 3 translates from v’s into the usual grid. Have we met that? Yes: part 1’s change-of-coordinates matrix, P. Its columns are v₁ and v₂.
Step 1 goes the other way. What is it? P undone. Call it P⁻¹.

Does it undo P? Yes. P⁻¹ takes (2, 0) to (1, −1), and P takes (1, −1) back to (2, 0).
Why the −1? As 3⁻¹ = ⅓ undoes multiplying by 3. Say “P inverse”.
Step 2 only stretches. What is it? D, a matrix with the eigenvalues on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere: a diagonal matrix.

Why is P⁻¹ on the right, when it’s step 1? A matrix acts on what’s to its right, so P D P⁻¹ x is read right to left: P⁻¹ first, P last.

Writing A = P D P⁻¹ is called diagonalizing A (Lay 5.3).

NoteThe Law of Stretching

Use a matrix’s eigenvectors as the basis, and the matrix only stretches. A = P D P⁻¹: find the coordinates, stretch them, change back.

Why anyone bothers

What is A applied ten times to x? Ten matrix multiplications, if done the long way.
And in v’s? Stretch the coordinates ten times: (3¹⁰·1, 1¹⁰·(−1)) = (59049, −1).
So what is A¹⁰x? 59049·(1, 1) − 1·(−1, 1) = (59050, 59048).
How much work was that? One look-up, one power of each number, one translation back.

Lay’s 5.3, Example 2 does the same with another matrix:

What is its k-th power? P Dᵏ P⁻¹. Only the 5ᵏ and the 3ᵏ change.

Same map, new matrix

Part 1 changed the basis and kept the arrow. Now we change the basis and keep the map.

In the usual grid, A’s matrix is (2 1; 1 2). In v’s, what is it? D = (3 0; 0 1). In v’s, A only stretches.
Are A and D two different maps? No. One map, written in two bases. Lay calls such matrices similar.
What changed between them? The entries.
What didn’t? What belongs to the map itself: the eigenvalues, 3 and 1, for a start.

One more number belongs to the map: how much it scales area.

What does A do to the unit square? Makes the parallelogram on (2, 1) and (1, 2), of area 2·2 − 1·1 = 3.
And D? Makes a 3 × 1 rectangle: area 3. The same, because it’s the same map.
What is that number called? The determinant. For (a b; c d), det = ad − bc.

To check your understanding: a friend says A’s eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, 2 and 2. Are they right? Decide before you read on.

Is 2 an eigenvalue of A? No. A’s eigenvalues are 3 and 1.
When are the diagonal entries the eigenvalues? When the matrix is diagonal, like D. Entries depend on the basis; eigenvalues don’t.
NoteThe Law of Invariance

A change of basis changes a matrix’s entries, not the map. What belongs to the map survives it: its eigenvalues, and its determinant.

Finding the eigenvalues yourself

So far, 3 and 1 were handed to you. Here is where they come from. I is the identity, (1 0; 0 1), the matrix that changes nothing.

If v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, what does A − λI do to v? Av − λv = λv − λv = 0. It flattens v to 0.
A matrix that flattens an arrow to 0 squashes the square onto a line. What area is left? 0. So det(A − λI) = 0.
For our A, what is A − λI? (2−λ 1; 1 2−λ), so det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)² − 1.
When is (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0? When 2 − λ = 1 or −1: λ = 1 or λ = 3.
Check λ = 3. A − 3I = (−1 1; 1 −1) sends (1, 1) to (0, 0): the eigenvector, flattened.

det(A − λI) = 0 is Lay’s characteristic equation (5.2).

Not every matrix is so kind

What is S(1, 0)? (1, 0). Not turned.
What is S(0, 1)? (1, 1). Turned.
Which arrows does S not turn? Only those along (1, 0). One line.
How many basis vectors does a flat page need? Two.
So can we write S = P D P⁻¹? No. There aren’t enough eigenvectors.
Look back at A’s v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1). Notice anything? They are perpendicular.
Is that luck? No. A is symmetric: it is its own mirror across the diagonal. That is part 3.
And what about S? Use two different bases, one for the arrow going in and one for the arrow coming out. That is SVD, part 4.

In Lay

Section and example numbers from [Lay16].

Here Lay
own arrows eigenvectors (5.1)
how much each stretches eigenvalues (5.1)
A = P D P⁻¹ diagonalization; the Diagonalization Theorem (5.3)
A¹⁰x by stretching powers, Aᵏ = P Dᵏ P⁻¹ (5.3)
P⁻¹ the inverse matrix (2.2)
S has too few eigenvectors S is not diagonalizable (5.3)
A and D: one map, two matrices similar matrices; same eigenvalues, 5.2 Theorem 4
area scale, ad − bc the determinant; area = |det A|, 3.3 Theorem 9
det(A − λI) = 0 the characteristic equation (5.2)

item.title: Linear algebra 3: coordinates that measure
item.description:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.

Part 2 found A’s two eigenvectors:

It ended with a hint: they are perpendicular. This part is about why that matters. In a perpendicular basis, a coordinate stops being a bookkeeping number and becomes a measurement.

A coordinate that depends on its neighbours

Both pictures have the same x = (6, 4) and the same b₁ = (4, 1). What changed? Only b₂: (−6, 1) on the left, (0, 1) on the right.
How much b₁ is in x, on the left? 3, part 1’s coordinates: x = 3b₁ + b₂.
And on the right? 1.5: 1.5·(4, 1) + 2.5·(0, 1) = (6, 4).
b₁ didn’t move. Why did its coordinate change? Coordinates are found together, by solving a·b₁ + b·b₂ = x. Move b₂, and a must change to make up for it.
So is “how much b₁ is in x” a question about x and b₁? No. It’s a question about the whole basis.
Can a coordinate depend only on x and its own direction? Yes, when the basis vectors are perpendicular.

Solving like this is how Lay finds coordinates in 4.4, Example 4: b₁ = (2, 1), b₂ = (−1, 1), x = (4, 5); 2a − b = 4 and a + b = 5 give . Those b’s aren’t perpendicular, so solving was the only way.

Shadows

Take x = (2, 0). Drop a line from x’s tip straight onto v₁’s line, at a right angle. Where does it land? At (1, 1). That is 1·v₁.
And straight onto v₂’s line? At (1, −1). That is −1·v₂.
Are (1, −1) x’s coordinates in v’s? Yes: 1·(1, 1) − 1·(−1, 1) = (2, 0).
Why did dropping a line work? x is made of some v₁ and some v₂. The v₂ part is perpendicular to v₁’s line, so it adds nothing there.
What is that landing point called? x’s shadow on the line.

The shadow is a picture. Here are the official words, the ones Lay uses (6.1–6.2):

  • the shadow is the orthogonal projection of x onto v₁’s line;
  • orthogonal is the mathematician’s word for perpendicular.

From here on, we say projection and orthogonal.

To find a projection without drawing, use the dot product (Lay also calls it the inner product): multiply matching numbers and add.

What is x·v₁? (2, 0)·(1, 1) = 2·1 + 0·1 = 2.
And v₁·v₁? 1 + 1 = 2.
How much v₁ is in x? x·v₁ divided by v₁·v₁: 2/2 = 1.
And how much v₂? x·v₂ = −2, v₂·v₂ = 2, so −1.
What does a dot product of 0 mean? Orthogonal: the projection lands at 0. Check v₁·v₂ = −1 + 1 = 0.
NoteThe Law of Measurement

When the basis is orthogonal, each coordinate is a measurement of x along one direction: (x·v) / (v·v). It depends on x and v, and on nothing else.

So what is x’s coordinate along v₁ now? A measurement: how far x reaches along v₁. v₂ never comes into it.
Is it quicker, too? One dot product per coordinate, no equations. The speed comes from the independence.

Now try it yourself. The faint path walks x’s coordinates: so much v₁, then so much v₂. The ring is x’s coordinate along v₁; the dot is its projection onto v₁. Drag the tip of x: while v₁ and v₂ are orthogonal, ring and dot stay together. Then tilt v₂: the ring slides away, and the dot stays put.

V1C = "#7570b3"   // v₁ and its projection (purple)
V2C = "#d95f02"   // v₂ and its projection (orange)
dot = (a, b) => a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1]

viewof sh = {
  const X0 = -4, X1 = 5, Y0 = -4, Y1 = 4, S = 44;       // S px per unit
  const W = (X1 - X0) * S, H = (Y1 - Y0) * S;
  const px = p => [(p[0] - X0) * S, (Y1 - p[1]) * S];
  const fromPx = (u, w) => [Math.round(u / S + X0), Math.round(Y1 - w / S)];
  const v1 = [1, 1];
  const state = {x: [2, 0], v2: [-1, 1]};
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", `${W}px`)
    .style("touch-action", "none");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  for (const [id, color] of [["s3a", V1C], ["s3b", V2C], ["s3x", "black"]])
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 9).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5)
      .attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10z").attr("fill", color);
  const g = svg.append("g");
  const node = svg.node();
  function seg(p, q, color, width, opts = {}) {
    const [a, b] = [px(p), px(q)];
    const l = g.append("line").attr("x1", a[0]).attr("y1", a[1])
      .attr("x2", b[0]).attr("y2", b[1]).attr("stroke", color)
      .attr("stroke-width", width).attr("stroke-opacity", opts.opacity ?? 1);
    if (opts.tip) l.attr("marker-end", `url(#${opts.tip})`);
    if (opts.dash) l.attr("stroke-dasharray", "5,4");
  }
  function dotAt(p, color, r = 6, handle = false) {
    const [a, b] = px(p);
    g.append("circle").attr("cx", a).attr("cy", b).attr("r", r)
      .attr("fill", color).attr("fill-opacity", handle ? 0.3 : 1)
      .style("cursor", handle ? "grab" : null);
  }
  function label(p, text, color) {
    const [a, b] = px(p);
    g.append("text").attr("x", a + 9).attr("y", b - 9).attr("fill", color)
      .attr("font-size", 17).text(text);
  }
  function draw() {
    g.selectAll("*").remove();
    for (let k = X0; k <= X1; k++) seg([k, Y0], [k, Y1], "#999", 0.7, {opacity: 0.2});
    for (let k = Y0; k <= Y1; k++) seg([X0, k], [X1, k], "#999", 0.7, {opacity: 0.2});
    const {x, v2} = state;
    for (const [v, c] of [[v1, V1C], [v2, V2C]])
      seg([-20 * v[0], -20 * v[1]], [20 * v[0], 20 * v[1]], c, 1.5, {opacity: 0.35});
    // the coordinate: walk a of v1, then b of v2, to x (as in part 1)
    const det = v1[0] * v2[1] - v2[0] * v1[1];
    const a = (x[0] * v2[1] - v2[0] * x[1]) / det;
    const b = (v1[0] * x[1] - x[0] * v1[1]) / det;
    const mid = [a * v1[0], a * v1[1]];
    seg([0, 0], mid, V1C, 3, {opacity: 0.5});
    seg(mid, x, V2C, 3, {opacity: 0.5});
    // the projection: drop straight from x onto v1's line
    const t = dot(x, v1) / dot(v1, v1), foot = [t * v1[0], t * v1[1]];
    seg(x, foot, "#666", 1.2, {dash: true});
    dotAt(foot, V1C);
    const [ma, mb] = px(mid);                      // ring: the coordinate
    g.append("circle").attr("cx", ma).attr("cy", mb).attr("r", 9)
      .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", V1C).attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
    seg([0, 0], x, "black", 3.5, {tip: "s3x"});
    seg([0, 0], v1, V1C, 4.5, {tip: "s3a"});
    seg([0, 0], v2, V2C, 4.5, {tip: "s3b"});
    dotAt(x, "black", 10, true); dotAt(v2, V2C, 10, true);
    label(x, "x", "black"); label(v1, "v₁", V1C); label(v2, "v₂", V2C);
    node.value = {x: [...x], v2: [...v2]};
    node.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  }
  let dragging = null;
  const local = e => {
    const r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
    return [(e.clientX - r.left) * W / r.width, (e.clientY - r.top) * H / r.height];
  };
  node.addEventListener("pointerdown", e => {
    const [u, w] = local(e);
    const dist = k => Math.hypot(px(state[k])[0] - u, px(state[k])[1] - w);
    const k = dist("x") < dist("v2") ? "x" : "v2";
    if (dist(k) < 26) { dragging = k; node.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointermove", e => {
    if (!dragging) return;
    const p = fromPx(...local(e));
    if (p[0] === 0 && p[1] === 0) return;
    if (dragging === "v2" && p[0] * v1[1] - p[1] * v1[0] === 0) return; // not along v₁
    if (p[0] !== state[dragging][0] || p[1] !== state[dragging][1]) {
      state[dragging] = p; draw();
    }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointerup", () => { dragging = null; });
  draw();
  return node;
}
// x's coordinate along v1 (solved with v2) beside its projection
// measurement (x.v1)/(v1.v1), which never looks at v2.
{
  const v1 = [1, 1], {x, v2} = sh;
  const det = v1[0] * v2[1] - v2[0] * v1[1];
  const a = (x[0] * v2[1] - v2[0] * x[1]) / det;
  const s1 = dot(x, v1) / dot(v1, v1);
  const f = n => (Number.isInteger(n) ? `${n}` : n.toFixed(2)).replace("-", "−");
  const perp = dot(v1, v2) === 0;
  return html`<div style="font-size:1.15em; font-family:monospace">
    v₁·v₂ = ${f(dot(v1, v2))}<br>
    coordinate along v₁, the ring (solved, uses v₂): <span style="color:${V1C}">${f(a)}</span><br>
    projection onto v₁, the dot (x and v₁ only):  <span style="color:${V1C}">${f(s1)}</span></div>
    <p>${perp
      ? html`<b>Orthogonal:</b> the coordinate is the measurement.`
      : Math.abs(a - s1) < 1e-9
        ? "Not orthogonal, but this x happens to agree. Move x."
        : html`<b>Not orthogonal:</b> the ring moved with v₂; the dot didn't.`}</p>`;
}

Lay writes the projection itself, the point where the dropped line lands, with a hat:

the coordinate times the vector. Try his 6.2, Example 3, with x = (7, 6) and v = (4, 2).

What is x·v? 7·4 + 6·2 = 40.
And v·v? 16 + 4 = 20. So the coordinate along v is 2.
What is x̂? 2v = (8, 4).
How far is x from v’s line? x − x̂ = (−1, 2), of length √(1 + 4) = √5. That is his Example 4.

Lengths come out right

A measurement should also get lengths right. Does a coordinate?

In part 1’s basis, x = (6, 4) has coordinates (3, 1). What is 3² + 1²? 10.
What is x’s length squared, 6² + 4²? 52. Those coordinates don’t know how long x is.
In our v’s, x = (2, 0) has coordinates (1, −1). What is 1² + (−1)²? 2. But x’s length squared is 4. Closer, still wrong.
Why? Each v has length √2, not 1. A coordinate counts v’s, and each v is longer than a unit.

So make each basis vector length 1. Dividing each v by its length, which Lay writes ‖v‖ = √(v·v) (6.1), here √2, is called normalizing; the result is a unit vector. Call them u₁ and u₂. Orthogonal and of length 1, they are orthonormal.

What are x’s coordinates in u’s? Measure: x·u₁ = 2/√2 = √2, and x·u₂ = −2/√2 = −√2. No dividing by u·u, which is 1.
What is (√2)² + (−√2)²? 2 + 2 = 4. x’s length squared, at last.
Is that luck? No. It is Pythagoras: x is √2 of u₁ plus −√2 of u₂, at a right angle.
Do angles come out right too? Yes. Dot products of coordinates equal dot products of the arrows, and angles come from dot products.
NoteThe Law of Length

In an orthonormal basis, ‖x‖² is the sum of the squares of x’s coordinates. Lengths and angles read off the coordinates are the true ones.

An orthonormal basis is a turned grid

Put u₁ and u₂ in a matrix as columns. Lay keeps the name P, as in part 2; the difference is that its columns now have length 1:

What is Pᵀ? P’s columns laid down as rows. Say “P transpose”.
What does Pᵀ do to x? Each row is a u, so each entry is a measurement x·u: x’s coordinates in u’s.
So what undoes P? Pᵀ. In part 2, P⁻¹ had to be worked out; here it is P read sideways.
Look back at part 2’s P⁻¹, (½ ½; −½ ½). What was it? The v’s as rows, halved: the measurements, divided by v·v = 2.
What does P do to the page? Turns it by 45°: it sends (1, 0) to u₁. Pᵀ turns it back.
What does a turn keep? More than any other change of basis: eigenvalues and area, as every change of basis does (part 2), and lengths and angles too.
What does Lay call such a P? An orthogonal matrix: square, orthonormal columns, P⁻¹ = Pᵀ. In 6.2 he names one U.

Part 2’s three steps become turn back, stretch, turn:

In the second picture, where are u₁ and u₂? Along the usual grid. Pᵀ turned them there.
What does D do to the circle? Stretches it three times wider, along u₁.
And the last step? P turns everything back. x lands at (4, 2), as in part 2.
NoteThe Law of the Turn

An orthonormal basis is the usual grid, turned. A = P D Pᵀ: turn back, stretch, turn. A symmetric matrix is a pure stretch along perpendicular axes.

Why A’s eigenvectors are orthogonal

A is symmetric: flip it across its diagonal and it is unchanged. The 1 above the diagonal matches the 1 below it.

We’ll work out one number, (Av₁)·v₂, in two ways.

First way: A stretches v₁ by 3. So what is (Av₁)·v₂? 3(v₁·v₂).
Second way: move A across the dot, onto v₂. Is (Av₁)·v₂ the same as v₁·(Av₂)? For symmetric A, yes. That’s the one fact we need; it’s checked below.
A stretches v₂ by 1. So what is v₁·(Av₂)? 1(v₁·v₂).
Both ways give the same number. So 3(v₁·v₂) = v₁·v₂. Which number is three times itself? Only 0. So v₁·v₂ = 0: orthogonal.

Why can A move across the dot? Write out both sides for any v and w:

Multiply out. Which terms does each line have? Both have 2v₁w₁, 2v₂w₂, v₂w₁ and v₁w₂. Equal.
Which number did that rely on? The two orange 1s being the same: A’s symmetry.
What if A were part 4’s matrix (3 0; 4 5)? Its corners differ (0 and 4), the two sides differ, and its eigenvectors aren’t orthogonal.
NoteThe Law of Symmetry

A symmetric matrix can move across a dot product. So its eigenvectors, with different eigenvalues, are orthogonal.

To check your understanding, here is Lay’s 7.1, Example 4:

Is it symmetric? Yes: the 2 above the diagonal matches the 2 below it.
Where does it send (2, 1)? And (−1, 2)? To (16, 8) = 8·(2, 1), and to (−3, 6) = 3·(−1, 2). Eigenvectors, with eigenvalues 8 and 3.
Are they orthogonal? (2, 1)·(−1, 2) = −2 + 2 = 0. Yes, as the Law says.

Keep only the biggest part

A measurement lets us do one more thing: throw coordinates away. Back to part 1’s x = (6, 4), and keep only what lies along b₁ = (4, 1).

In part 1’s basis, x’s b₁ part is 3b₁. Where is it? (12, 3), about 6.1 from x. Far off.
Now take x’s projection onto b₁’s line instead. Where is it? (28/17)·(4, 1), about (6.6, 1.6): about 2.4 from x.
Is any point on that line closer to x? No. The dashed line meets it at a right angle, so the projection is the nearest point.
Which basis keeps exactly that point? An orthonormal one with u₁ along b₁. Its first coordinate is a measurement, so keeping it alone is as close as that direction can get.
NoteThe Law of the Nearest Point

In an orthonormal basis, keep only some coordinates, and you get the nearest point those directions can reach: the projection.

Do these three laws need A to be symmetric? No. Measuring, lengths and nearest points hold in any orthonormal basis. Symmetry only makes A’s eigenvectors one.
Most matrices aren’t symmetric. Is that the end? No. Part 4 gives every matrix an orthonormal basis going in and another coming out, then uses the nearest point to find the best line through data.

In Lay

Section and example numbers from [Lay16].

Here Lay
shadow orthogonal projection, x̂ (6.2; he writes ŷ)
perpendicular orthogonal (6.1)
dot product inner product, u·v (6.1)
a coordinate is a measurement, (x·v)/(v·v) the weights, 6.2 Theorem 5
length, made 1 ‖v‖, normalizing, unit vector (6.1)
orthogonal, length 1 orthonormal (6.2)
the Law of Length 6.2 Theorem 7: ‖Ux‖ = ‖x‖, (Ux)·(Uy) = x·y
P, with P⁻¹ = Pᵀ orthogonal matrix; U in 6.2 (6.2, 7.1)
A = P D Pᵀ orthogonally diagonalizable (7.1)
the Law of Symmetry 7.1 Theorem 1
every symmetric matrix has one the Spectral Theorem (7.1)
the Law of the Nearest Point the Best Approximation Theorem, 6.3 Theorem 9

item.title: Linear algebra 4: two orthogonal bases
item.description:
Cover the right-hand column. Answer each question in your head, then look.

Part 3 ended with a promise: an orthogonal basis for every matrix. Here is one that isn’t symmetric:

Its eigenvectors aren’t enough

Is A symmetric? No. Its first row is (3, 0); its first column is (3, 4).
What is A(0, 1)? (0, 5). Stretched by 5, not turned.
What is A(1, −2)? (3, −6). Stretched by 3, not turned.
So (0, 1) and (1, −2) are eigenvectors of A. Are they orthogonal? (0, 1)·(1, −2) = −2. No.
Then can we find coordinates by projection? No. Part 3’s opening picture showed why.
And the shear S = (1 1; 0 1) from part 2? Worse: only one line of eigenvectors.

So we ask for less. We don’t need an arrow to keep its line. We need two orthogonal arrows going in that come out still orthogonal.

Orthogonal in, orthogonal out

Drag the tip of v₁ around the circle. v₂ stays a quarter turn ahead of it. On the right, A sends the circle to an ellipse, and v₁, v₂ to Av₁, Av₂.

A = [[3, 0], [4, 5]]
V1 = "#7570b3"   // v₁ and Av₁ (purple)
V2 = "#d95f02"   // v₂ and Av₂ (orange)
mul = (A, p) => [A[0][0] * p[0] + A[0][1] * p[1],
                 A[1][0] * p[0] + A[1][1] * p[1]]

viewof angle = {
  const S = 22, R = Math.SQRT2;                     // S px per unit
  const L = {x0: -2.5, x1: 2.5, y0: -2.5, y1: 2.5}; // the "in" panel
  const Rt = {x0: -7, x1: 7, y0: -10, y1: 10};      // the "out" panel
  const wL = (L.x1 - L.x0) * S, wR = (Rt.x1 - Rt.x0) * S;
  const W = wL + 30 + wR, H = (Rt.y1 - Rt.y0) * S;
  const pxL = p => [(p[0] - L.x0) * S, H / 2 - p[1] * S];
  const pxR = p => [wL + 30 + (p[0] - Rt.x0) * S, H / 2 - p[1] * S];
  let deg = 0;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", `${W}px`)
    .style("touch-action", "none");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  for (const [id, color] of [["s4a", V1], ["s4b", V2]])
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 9).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5)
      .attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10z").attr("fill", color);
  const g = svg.append("g");
  const node = svg.node();
  function arrow(px, q, color, tip) {
    const [a, b] = px([0, 0]), [c, d] = px(q);
    g.append("line").attr("x1", a).attr("y1", b).attr("x2", c).attr("y2", d)
      .attr("stroke", color).attr("stroke-width", 4)
      .attr("marker-end", `url(#${tip})`);
  }
  function curve(px, pts) {
    g.append("path").attr("d", d3.line()(pts.map(px)))
      .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#999").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  }
  function draw() {
    g.selectAll("*").remove();
    const t = deg * Math.PI / 180;
    const v1 = [R * Math.cos(t), R * Math.sin(t)];
    const v2 = [-v1[1], v1[0]];
    const ring = d3.range(0, 361, 3).map(a => a * Math.PI / 180)
      .map(a => [R * Math.cos(a), R * Math.sin(a)]);
    curve(pxL, ring);
    curve(pxR, ring.map(p => mul(A, p)));
    arrow(pxL, v2, V2, "s4b"); arrow(pxL, v1, V1, "s4a");
    arrow(pxR, mul(A, v2), V2, "s4b"); arrow(pxR, mul(A, v1), V1, "s4a");
    const [a, b] = pxL(v1);
    g.append("circle").attr("cx", a).attr("cy", b).attr("r", 9)
      .attr("fill", V1).attr("fill-opacity", 0.3).style("cursor", "grab");
    for (const [px, p, txt, c] of [[pxL, v1, "v₁", V1], [pxL, v2, "v₂", V2],
        [pxR, mul(A, v1), "Av₁", V1], [pxR, mul(A, v2), "Av₂", V2]]) {
      const [u, w] = px(p);
      g.append("text").attr("x", u + 8).attr("y", w - 8).attr("fill", c)
        .attr("font-size", 16).text(txt);
    }
    node.value = deg;
    node.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  }
  let dragging = false;
  const local = e => {
    const r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
    return [(e.clientX - r.left) * W / r.width, (e.clientY - r.top) * H / r.height];
  };
  node.addEventListener("pointerdown", e => {
    const [u, w] = local(e);
    const t = deg * Math.PI / 180;
    const [a, b] = pxL([R * Math.cos(t), R * Math.sin(t)]);
    if (Math.hypot(a - u, b - w) < 24) {
      dragging = true; node.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
    }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointermove", e => {
    if (!dragging) return;
    const [u, w] = local(e), [cx, cy] = pxL([0, 0]);
    let d = Math.round(Math.atan2(cy - w, u - cx) * 180 / Math.PI / 5) * 5;
    d = (d + 360) % 360;                             // snap to 5°
    if (d !== deg) { deg = d; draw(); }
  });
  node.addEventListener("pointerup", () => { dragging = false; });
  draw();
  return node;
}
{
  const t = angle * Math.PI / 180;
  const v1 = [Math.cos(t), Math.sin(t)], v2 = [-v1[1], v1[0]];
  const a = mul(A, v1), b = mul(A, v2);
  const cos = (a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1]) / Math.hypot(...a) / Math.hypot(...b);
  const between = Math.round(Math.acos(cos) * 180 / Math.PI);
  return html`<div style="font-size:1.2em; font-family:monospace">
    v₁ at ${angle}°  →  Av₁ and Av₂ at ${between}° to each other</div>
    <p>${between === 90
      ? html`<b>Orthogonal in, orthogonal out.</b>
        Av₁ and Av₂ lie along the ellipse's long and short axes.`
      : "Not orthogonal yet. Keep turning."}</p>`;
}
Turn v₁. Are Av₁ and Av₂ usually orthogonal? No.
When are they? With v₁ at 45°, along (1, 1), or a quarter turn from there.
Check without the picture: what are A(1, 1) and A(−1, 1)? (3, 9) and (−3, 1).
Are those orthogonal? (3, 9)·(−3, 1) = −9 + 9 = 0. Yes.
Where are they on the ellipse? Along its long axis and its short axis.
How much did v₁ stretch? ‖(3, 9)‖ = √90 and ‖(1, 1)‖ = √2. So √45, about 6.7.
And v₂? ‖(−3, 1)‖ / ‖(−1, 1)‖ = √10 / √2 = √5, about 2.2.
What are these stretches called? Singular values, σ₁ and σ₂ (σ is Greek s, “sigma”).

The three steps, once more

Take x = (2, 0) again. In comes v₁ = (1, 1) and v₂ = (−1, 1); out go u₁ along (3, 9) and u₂ along (−3, 1).

Step 1: x’s coordinates in v’s? By projection, since the v’s are orthogonal: 2/2 = 1 of v₁, −2/2 = −1 of v₂.
Step 2: what does A do to each basis vector? Sends v₁ to (3, 9), and v₂ to (−3, 1).
Step 3: so where does x go? 1·(3, 9) − 1·(−3, 1) = (6, 8).
Check the long way: A(2, 0)? (3·2 + 0·0, 4·2 + 5·0) = (6, 8). The same.
In part 3, the same P turned back and turned again. Here? Two different turns: V for the arrow going in, U for the arrow coming out.

Make every basis vector length 1 (orthonormal), as in part 3, and the steps become three matrices:

Read right to left: what does Vᵀ do? Projects x onto the v’s: x’s coordinates in v’s.
And Σ? Stretches each coordinate, by σ₁ and σ₂.
And U? Builds the result from the u’s.
What does Lay call the v’s and the u’s? The right and left singular vectors (7.4).
Why insist that both bases are orthonormal? So every coordinate, going in and coming out, is a measurement (part 3): lengths survive, and keeping the biggest σ’s gives the nearest approximation.
How is this different from part 2’s P D P⁻¹? Two bases instead of one.
Does every matrix have one? Yes, every one. Even the shear S: its v₁ leans at about 58°, and its σ’s are 1.618 and 0.618.
NoteThe Law of Two Bases

Every matrix sends some orthogonal arrows to orthogonal arrows. A = U Σ Vᵀ: project onto the v’s, stretch, build with the u’s. This is the singular value decomposition, SVD.

Where the v’s come from

We found 45° by turning v₁ until it worked. There is a shortcut, and it uses part 3.

Is AᵀA symmetric? Yes. Row 1 is (25, 20); so is column 1.
So what do we know about its eigenvectors? Part 3: they are orthogonal.
What are they? (1, 1), eigenvalue 45, and (−1, 1), eigenvalue 5. Our v’s.
And 45 and 5? σ₁² and σ₂².

What survives, and what’s lost

In A = UΣVᵀ, which part changes area? Only Σ. The turns keep area.
So what is det A, up to sign? σ₁σ₂ = √45·√5 = 15. Check: 3·5 − 0·4 = 15.
What if a σ is 0? That direction is flattened to 0.

Take F = (1 1; 1 1). What is F(1, −1)? (0, 0).
What are F’s σ’s? 2 and 0. The circle goes flat, onto a segment.
Can any matrix undo F? No. F sends (1, −1) and (0, 0) to the same place; nothing can tell them apart again.
What does Lay call the number of nonzero σ’s? The rank (7.4). F has rank 1.
And the flattened directions? The null space (4.2).

Why anyone bothers: the best line

Part 3 ended with the nearest point: in an orthonormal basis, keeping one coordinate gives the projection, as close as that direction can get. Now we choose the direction.

Read A’s rows as two points, (3, 0) and (4, 5).

For a length-1 arrow v, what are the two numbers in Av? Row 1 dotted with v, and row 2 dotted with v: each point’s projection onto v’s line, as a signed length.
Which v makes Av longest? v₁. A stretches it most: the long axis of the ellipse.
So which line gets the longest projections? The one along v₁ = (1, 1).
Why is that the line closest to the points? Each point’s length is fixed. Projection² + distance² = length², so the longer the projection, the shorter the distance.
And with a thousand rows? The same: v₁ is the line through the origin that passes closest to all of them.
NoteThe Law of the Best Line

A’s first in-arrow v₁ is the line that passes closest to A’s rows.

Make each row a photo of a face, and v₁, v₂, … become the “eigenfaces” that most faces are mostly made of. That story is told in the SVD comic, which follows Hopcroft and Kannan from best fit to principal components.

In Lay

Section and example numbers from [Lay16].

Here Lay
v₁, v₂, going in right singular vectors (7.4)
u₁, u₂, coming out left singular vectors (7.4)
the stretches σ singular values: square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA (7.4)
A = U Σ Vᵀ the singular value decomposition (7.4)
circle to ellipse; v₁ stretched most 7.4, Example 1; the largest ‖Ax‖ for unit x (7.3)
|det A| = σ₁σ₂ the determinant as area (3.3)
the number of nonzero σ’s rank, 7.4 Theorem 9
the flattened directions the null space, Nul A (4.2)
the best line through the rows principal components (7.5)

item.title: Lesson 3: functions that take more than one thing
item.description:
My drawing, made to talk with Runway Act-Two. Later in the course: how.

Lesson 1 gave you def and return with one input (parity). Lesson 2 gave you while, input() and f-strings. This lesson uses all of them. What is new: a function’s name, several inputs, how to pass those inputs (by position or by name), the difference between return and print, one function that calls another, and a function that wraps a call to Claude.

Name it, then call it (15 min session)

Left pane, you work. Right pane, Claude is your tutor.

A function is a name for a computation

A function is a name for a computation: a recipe, a process, a rule you want to use again without writing it out again. Naming it well is the most important habit in this lesson. A good name says what the step is for, so the reader does not have to work out how it was made.

Lesson 1’s recipe took one input, n, and gave back a word. A recipe usually needs more than one input: the amount, the servings it was written for, and the servings you want. The three names in the parentheses after def are parameters: the boxes the function fills when you call it.

Type this into ~/course/scale.py. You will keep using this file:

def scaled(amount, base_servings, servings):
    return amount * servings / base_servings

print(f"Flour: {250 * 6 / 2} g")
print(f"Flour: {scaled(250, 2, 6)} g")

Both lines print 750.0 g. The first only says how the number was made; the second says what it means.

To check your understanding, ask Claude in the right pane: “Suggest three names for a function that turns a recipe’s base amount into the amount for any number of servings. Which name is best, and why?” Guess its top pick first.

Names or positions for the inputs

A call can pass its inputs in two ways:

  • by position: scaled(250, 2, 6). Each value goes to the next parameter, in order.
  • by name: scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=6). Each value goes to the parameter with that name, in any order.

Use names when a wrong order would still run and still give an answer. Here the program does not stop when you swap two numbers. It prints 83.33333333333333 instead of 750.0, and nothing tells you it is wrong. The names make that mistake hard to make.

Use positions when the order is obvious and the call is short. parity(7) from lesson 1 has one input, so there is no order to get wrong.

Rule of thumb: if the reader would need to look up the function to know which value is which, name the inputs.

Which would you use, names or positions, for scaled with its three numbers, and for parity with its one? Then check your answers against the rule above.

A recipe that scales (20 min session)

Now name the inputs in every call. Keep scale.py from the start of the lesson, and add these lines to it:

print(f"{scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=4)} g flour")
print(f"{scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=1)} g flour")

Guess what the first line prints. Note that / always gives a decimal (lesson 1), so check the second line too.

To check your understanding: what does scaled(amount=250, base_servings=4, servings=2) print, and why is it different from the first line? Decide before you read on.

It prints 125.0. The recipe is now written for 4 servings, and you want 2, so the amount halves. Moving the names around changes nothing; changing the numbers does. Run it, or ask Claude in the right pane why.

NoteTry it yourself

Write a second function, flour_for, that calls scaled with 250 grams for 2 servings and a number of servings you choose as its one input. It should return the amount of flour. Guess its output before you run it.

Reuse with input in the middle

One function can serve many ingredients, and the number can come from the user while the program is running. Add these lines to scale.py, below scaled:

servings = int(input("How many servings? "))
print(f"Flour: {scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=servings)} g")
print(f"Sugar: {scaled(amount=100, base_servings=2, servings=servings)} g")

Guess the two lines for 6, then run it and check. Then type 1. You wrote the rule once, in scaled, and it worked for two ingredients, with a number the program didn’t know until you typed it.

Bug hunt: a recipe that prints instead

Claude wrote this version. It has one bug. Type it in scale_bug.py, run it, and find the bug. Claude will not say where it is.

def scaled(amount, base_servings, servings):
    print(amount * servings / base_servings)

total = scaled(amount=250, base_servings=2, servings=4) + 100
print(f"total: {total}")

For the bug:

  1. Write down the error message.
  2. Guess what is wrong, in one sentence.
  3. Fix it, run it, and check the output by hand.

Then tell Claude, in the right pane, what you found, and ask only why the error happens.

Functions that call functions (25 min session)

A function can call another function, the same way your program calls input and print. Open ~/course/frame.py and type this:

def perimeter(width, height):
    return 2 * width + 2 * height

def frame_cost(width, height, price_per_cm):
    return perimeter(width, height) * price_per_cm

print(f"Frame: {frame_cost(width=40, height=50, price_per_cm=3)} euros")

Guess perimeter(40, 50) on its own, then what the last line prints. Run it and check.

To check your understanding, ask Claude in the right pane: “Where does frame_cost get the perimeter from, and why is that useful?” Guess the gist of its answer first.

The answer: it comes from perimeter. If the rule for a perimeter changes, you change it in one place, and frame_cost still works.

WarningOrder matters

Python runs a function body only when the function is called, but the functions must be defined above the line that calls them. Try moving print(...) above def perimeter. What error do you expect? Then run it.

AI thread: wrap the call in a function

Each time your program talks to Claude, the same lines repeat. Put them in one function, so the rest of the program only asks a question and gets a reply. Add this to frame.py, above the prints. Guess what the last line prints, then run it.

import subprocess

def ask(question):
    reply = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", question, "--tools", "",
         "--no-session-persistence"],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    return reply.stdout.strip()

print(ask("Reply with only the word hello."))

ask is the one place the program talks to Claude. If the call needs to change, for example a new flag, you change it here and nowhere else. ask returns the reply and does not print it: the caller decides what to do with it.

A function that calls ask

Lesson 2’s shape program asked Claude for a turn angle, then turned that text into a number. Put that step in a function, and it can be reused by any program that needs an angle:

def angle_for(shape):
    reply = ask(f"How many degrees does a turtle turn at each corner of a {shape}? Reply with only the number.")
    return float(reply)

print(f"Pentagon turn: {angle_for('pentagon')} degrees")
sides = round(360 / angle_for("pentagon"))
print(f"Sides: {sides}")

Guess what the first line prints, and what sides comes to. The first call to angle_for has the whole chain behind it: angle_for calls ask, and ask calls Claude.

To check your understanding, ask Claude in the right pane: “Why does angle_for call ask instead of calling subprocess itself?” Guess the gist of its answer first.

If Claude’s reply is a sentence, float fails inside angle_for, and the error points at float, not at the question. A function that hides a step also hides where it went wrong, so read the traceback to the bottom to see which function failed.

Write your own program

Write a program of your own with at least two functions, one of which calls the other. Claude writes none of it.

Pick a theme from cooking, art, music, or fashion, and build something that takes at least two inputs, returns a value, and prints a line at the end in your theme’s words. One of your functions must ask Claude for a reply and return it, using ask from the AI thread above.

Simple ideas to start from, pick one:

  • a function that prices a frame from its width and height, and a second one that adds tax;
  • a function that scales a dough or a paint mix for any number of batches;
  • a function that asks Claude for a short name for any number you give it, and returns the name.

Before you run it, guess the output for two different sets of inputs. Name the inputs in any call where a wrong order would still run.

When it works, walk Claude through it, line by line. Claude will ask why each function takes the inputs it takes, and where it could fail, for example with a zero or a negative number. Claude will not fix anything.

item.title: Lesson 2: loops, drawn and waiting
item.description:
My drawing, made to talk with Runway Act-Two. Later in the course: how.

Lesson 1 is the base: fish, nvim, cp, for, if, def, python3. None of that is explained again here; it is used. What is new: turtle drawing (import turtle), while, input(), int() and float(), f-strings, asking Claude from a program (subprocess), the shell’s Ctrl+C, and mv and rm.

If import turtle fails on your machine, run sudo apt install -y python3-tk (the Tk window library turtle uses). It worked here already, so you may not need it.

Draw a square with a loop (20 min session)

Left pane, you work. Right pane, Claude is your tutor.

Lesson 2 is about loops, so the first drawing is a loop you can see.

Open ~/course/square.py in nvim and type this. Before you run it, where do you think the turtle ends up, and which way will it face?

import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
for side in range(4):
    t.forward(100)
    t.left(90)

turtle.done()

Run it from fish:

python3 square.py

turtle.Turtle() makes a pen. forward(100) walks 100 steps and draws a line. left(90) turns 90 degrees to the left. turtle.done() keeps the window open until you close it. Ctrl+C stops it from the terminal.

Was your guess right? Where did the turtle end up?

To check your understanding: what would the picture look like if the loop ran 3 times instead of 4? Decide before you read on.

It draws three sides, a U shape, and the turtle stops one side short of where it started. The turns of 90 degrees only close the shape when there are four of them.

NoteTry it yourself

Change the loop so it draws a square with sides of 50. Then draw a row of three squares side by side. Where do you think each one starts? Guess before you run it. The change is in the lines inside the loop.

Colour and a row of squares

Add a colour before the loop:

t.color("blue")

Your guess: does the colour change the shape, or only the line? Run it and see.

Now draw the same square three times, with a for loop around the whole thing, and move the turtle between squares with t.penup(), t.forward(150) and t.pendown(). Where will the third square end up? Guess, then run it.

Ask Claude for the angle

A nonagon has nine sides, and the turn at each corner is 360 divided by nine. What number do you expect? Then add these lines to square.py, after the square’s loop and before turtle.done(). They use the pen t that the square already made. Running them on their own, as a new file, fails with NameError: name 't' is not defined:

import subprocess

reply = subprocess.run(
    ["claude", "-p", "How many degrees does a turtle turn at each corner of a nonagon? Reply with only the number.", "--no-session-persistence"],
    capture_output=True, text=True)
angle = float(reply.stdout.strip())
for side in range(9):
    t.forward(60)
    t.left(angle)

Was Claude’s number the one you predicted? The program does not know the answer; it trusts the reply and uses it. Your job is to check.

Aside: mv and rm

You have cp from lesson 1. Two more file commands finish the set. In ~/course, make a copy and move it:

cp square.py square2.py
mv square2.py shape.py
ls

Before ls, predict its output. Then remove the file:

rm shape.py
ls
Warningrm is permanent

mv replaces a file that already has the new name, without asking. rm removes a file with no trash and no u. Read the name twice before you press Enter.

Name a shape, and Claude gives its angle (25 min session)

Now input() drives the drawing. You type a shape’s name, Claude works out the turn at each corner, and the turtle draws it.

The question to Claude is an f-string: f"... {name} ..." puts the value of name into the text. You will use this form from now on. It replaces the + and str() joining you may have seen elsewhere.

import subprocess
import turtle

t = turtle.Turtle()
name = input("Name a shape (blank to stop): ")
while name != "":
    reply = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", f"How many degrees does a turtle turn at each corner of a {name}? Reply with only the number.", "--no-session-persistence"],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    angle = float(reply.stdout.strip())
    t.clear()
    for side in range(round(360 / angle)):
        t.forward(60)
        t.left(angle)
    name = input("Name a shape (blank to stop): ")
turtle.done()

Guess, for a pentagon, what turn Claude gives and how many sides the program draws. The line round(360 / angle) works out the sides from the angle.

Type pentagon, then hexagon, then press Enter on an empty line.

Bug hunt: a reply that is a sentence

Claude wrote this version, and it has one bug. Run it and find it. Claude will not say where it is.

import subprocess

reply = subprocess.run(
    ["claude", "-p", "How many degrees does a turtle turn at each corner of a nonagon? Reply with a sentence.", "--no-session-persistence"],
    capture_output=True, text=True)
angle = float(reply.stdout.strip())
print(angle)

For the bug:

  1. Write down the error message.
  2. Read what Claude sent back. Is it a number?
  3. Fix the program so it still works when Claude sends a sentence, or change what you ask. Decide which, and say why.

A playlist that asks Claude for lengths (25 min session)

Type song names. Claude gives each song’s length, and the program adds it to the running total. Run it first exactly as written, with no changes:

import subprocess

total = 0.0
song = input("Song name (blank to stop): ")
while song != "":
    reply = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", f"How many minutes long is the song {song}? Reply with only the number, like 3.5.", "--no-session-persistence"],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    minutes = float(reply.stdout.strip())
    total = total + minutes
    print(f"{song}: {minutes} min, so far {total} min")
    song = input("Song name (blank to stop): ")
print(f"playlist total: {total} minutes")

Guess what the first song’s line prints, and the total after two songs. Then type a real song you know, and a title that doesn’t exist.

Watch what comes back. It can be a number, a sentence, or a request to look through your files. Claude is an agent: it can look things up in your folders as well as answer from memory. The program only sees text, so it cannot tell which one happened. When it crashes, read the error, and ask Claude in the right pane: “Did you search my files to answer that?” Guess its answer first.

WarningSay no when it asks

If Claude asks permission to read a folder, say no unless you know why it needs that folder.

The correction: answers from memory only

The lookup needs only what Claude already knows, so turn the tools off. Add two items to the call, "--tools", "", like this:

reply = subprocess.run(
    ["claude", "-p", f"How many minutes long is the song {song}? Reply with only the number, like 3.5.", "--tools", "", "--no-session-persistence"],
    capture_output=True, text=True)

Run it again with the made-up title. Guess first: does Claude send back a number or a sentence now? --tools "" turns every tool off, so the call can only answer from memory. Claude may still be wrong, so the check below still matters.

Claude is only guessing at song lengths, so check one of them on a phone or a streaming app. Did Claude get it right?

Bug hunt: a playlist that stops at 3.5

Claude wrote this version, and it has one bug. Run it with a song that is 3.5 minutes long, and find the bug. Claude will not say where it is.

import subprocess

total = 0
song = input("Song name (blank to stop): ")
while song != "":
    reply = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", f"How many minutes long is the song {song}? Reply with only the number, like 3.5.", "--no-session-persistence"],
        capture_output=True, text=True)
    minutes = int(reply.stdout.strip())
    total = total + minutes
    print(f"{song}: {minutes} min, so far {total} min")
    song = input("Song name (blank to stop): ")
print(f"playlist total: {total} minutes")

For the bug:

  1. Write down the error message, and what Claude sent back.
  2. Guess why int fails on a decimal, in one sentence.
  3. Fix it, run it, and check the total by hand.

Write an agent (25 min session)

This time Claude is in the game. Write a guessing game where Claude is the guesser and your program is the referee. Claude writes none of the code; it only guesses.

Your program:

  • picks the secret, a number you choose in the code. Claude never sees it;
  • each turn, sends Claude the guesses and hints so far, and asks for its next guess with claude -p, with "--tools", "" as in the playlist session;
  • checks Claude’s reply: is it a number? is it right? is it too high or too low? (if, elif, else, and int());
  • stops when Claude is right, or after 5 turns, with a while loop;
  • prints one * per turn left with a for loop, and the result at the end.

Claude remembers nothing between calls, so your program must send the whole history every turn. That is the agent part: the program decides the next step, and the model only answers.

Before you run it, make a guess: how many turns does Claude need if the secret is 50, and does it guess 25 first?

Each run uses a few calls from the weekly budget, so run it once or twice, not ten times.

AI thread: let Claude pick the secret

Claude can pick the secret for you. Add this to the top of the guessing game, in a copy, and replace your secret line with it:

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ["claude", "-p", "Pick a secret whole number from 1 to 50. Reply with only the digits.", "--tools", "", "--no-session-persistence"],
    capture_output=True, text=True)
secret = int(result.stdout.strip())

Guess: will two runs of the game pick the same secret?

Each call to Claude remembers nothing about the last one. The secret survives only because it is stored in secret, a variable in your program. Guess what happens if you move the subprocess lines inside the while loop, then run it.

WarningBug hunt waiting in this one

Claude’s reply is text, not always just digits. If it answers Sure! 27, the int(...) line fails. Run the game several times until it does, read the error, and decide where a program should check what a model sent back.

item.title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
item.description:
Laura, from my drawing of Munch’s painting (1899), made to talk with Runway Act-Two. Later in the course: how.

Why are we doing this?

An AI can install software, add up numbers and write proofs faster than either of us ever will. So why learn any of it?

For the same reason people learned pure math long before anyone needed it. Almost nobody uses calculus at work. What it built was the ability to understand: to follow an argument, see why it holds, and notice when it doesn’t.

That’s the point of this course: not to get the computer to do things, but to understand what it did, and why, well enough to catch it when it’s wrong.

To check your understanding as you go, guess what each command will do before you run it. When the computer surprises you, that’s the interesting part: guess why, in your own words, check with Claude, and ask your teacher for help.

TipHow to use this page

This lesson is twelve short sessions, each one sitting of 15 to 30 minutes: setting up (the first three), Python (the next four), adding up 1 to 100 (three more) and Lean (the last two). Do one session, stop whenever you like, and come back: the list of sessions at the top of the page shows where you are and takes you back there.

Each grey box has a copy button in its top right corner. Paste into the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V and press Enter. Read the sentence above each box before you run it.

Turn on Linux (20 min session)

Turn on Linux (WSL)

Underneath the windows and buttons, a computer works with text. A terminal is a window where you talk to it in words. We’ll use Linux, running inside Windows (that’s WSL, Windows Subsystem for Linux).

  1. Click Start and type PowerShell.
  2. Right-click Windows PowerShell, choose Run as administrator, and click Yes.
  3. Paste this and press Enter:
wsl --install

When it says so, restart the computer. A window called Ubuntu (our kind of Linux) then opens and asks you to make up a username (short, lowercase, no spaces) and a password.

WarningThe password is invisible

When you type it, nothing appears, not even dots. That’s normal. Type it anyway and press Enter.

From now on, open Terminal from the Start menu and pick Ubuntu from the ▾ menu next to the tabs.

Look around

The line ending in $ is the prompt: the computer waiting for you.

pwd

pwd prints where you are, something like /home/anna: your home folder, written as a path (folders inside folders, separated by /).

mkdir course
cd course
pwd

Before the last line, guess what pwd will print now. (mkdir makes a folder, cd goes into one, cd .. goes up a level.)

Stop the password questions

Commands starting with sudo run as the administrator, and Linux asks for your password each time. The Windows login already protects this computer, so we tell Linux to stop asking:

echo "$USER ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/$USER
sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/$USER

Get a tutor (20 min session)

Your tutor: Claude Code

Claude is an AI, a language model: it learned from a huge amount of text to predict what words come next. That turns out to be enough to explain things and write code. It also makes Claude very good at sounding right. Usually it is right. Sometimes it isn’t, and it can’t always tell. That’s why you check.

Claude Code lets you talk to Claude in the terminal. You’ll need a Claude account.

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

curl downloads the installer, and | bash runs it (the |, a pipe, sends one command’s output into the next).

Claude could do this whole lesson by itself. That’s why we tell it not to. This box writes a file called CLAUDE.md: standing instructions Claude reads every time it starts in this folder.

cat > ~/course/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# Tutor mode

I'm a beginner learning to program, and above all to reason.
The point is that I work things out myself.
You're my tutor, not the one doing the work.

- Never write the code for my exercises,
  and don't run commands or edit files for me.
  If you solve it, the lesson is lost.
- If I paste an error message, explain in plain words
  what it means and where to look. One hint, not the fix.
- If I ask what a command does, explain it simply,
  then ask me to predict what will happen before I run it.
- Ask me "why?" often, and look for the hole
  in my explanations.
- If I ask how you work, or why AI gets things wrong,
  explain honestly and simply. That's part of the course.
- Allowed: if I ask for code *to referee*
  (with a hidden bug for me to find), write it.
- Keep answers short. Use everyday words.
EOF

Press Alt+Shift+D to split the window into two panes. In the right pane, start Claude:

cd ~/course
claude

The first time, it opens a browser to log in. Claude asks before it does anything on your computer: say no unless you understand what it’s asking.

Try two questions: “What did the cat > CLAUDE.md command I just ran do?” and “When are you most likely to be wrong?”

From now on: left pane, you work. Right pane, you ask.

TipAsking well

Claude only knows what you tell it. A good question says what you did, what happened, and what you think: “I ran python3 gauss.py and got this error: (paste). I think line 3 is wrong. Am I right?” Errors are normal. Read each one yourself first and guess, then paste it with your guess. Fixing it is your job.

A shell and an editor (25 min session)

A friendlier shell: fish

The program that reads what you type is the shell. Ubuntu’s is bash. We’ll use fish, which helps you type less. Ask Claude what chsh does, and predict what will change, and when:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y fish
sudo chsh -s /usr/bin/fish $USER

(apt installs software.) Close the left pane (exit) and open a new one with Alt+Shift+D. Was your prediction right?

Fish suggests the rest of a command in grey from what you typed before (→ accepts it), and Tab finishes names. ↑ brings back earlier commands.

Fish doesn’t know yet where Claude was installed. Tell it once:

fish_add_path ~/.local/bin

To check your understanding (ask Claude if you’re stuck): what is a “path”, and why did bash find Claude but fish didn’t?

An editor: nvim

To write programs we need a text editor. nvim runs inside the terminal.

sudo apt install -y neovim
cd ~/course
nvim hello.txt

nvim has two modes, and most nvim confusion is forgetting which one you’re in:

  • Normal mode, where it starts: every key is a command. x deletes a letter, u undoes. Type a word here and each letter does something, usually something strange.
  • Insert mode: keys type letters, like any other editor. The bottom line says -- INSERT --.

i goes from normal to insert; Esc goes back. Why two modes? So every key can be a command without holding Ctrl. When in doubt, press Esc: it always lands you in normal mode, and a second press does no harm.

Press (in normal mode) What it does
i start typing (insert mode)
Esc stop typing (from insert mode)
:wq Enter save and quit
:q! Enter quit without saving

Press i, type hello, press Esc, type :wq, press Enter. What will this print?

cat hello.txt

Everyone mistypes. In nvim, you fix things from normal mode:

Press (in normal mode) What it does
arrow keys move around
x delete the letter under the cursor
u undo (press again to undo more)
:5 Enter jump to line 5

To add letters, move to the spot and press i; Backspace works while you’re in insert mode.

Try it: nvim hello.txt, press x. Which letter goes? Then u to bring it back. Still in normal mode, type ox. Does x delete a letter again? Decide before you read on.

o is a command too: open a new line below and switch to insert mode. So the x after it is just a letter, on a new line. Esc, then u until it’s hello again, and :wq.

Stuck in nvim? Press Esc a few times, then :q!. (More nvim: type :Tutor inside it.)

Talk to Python (15 min session)

Python

python3

The prompt changes to >>>: you’re talking to Python now. Guess each answer before pressing Enter:

2 + 2
7 / 2
7 // 2
2 ** 10

Ask Claude why 7 / 2 and 7 // 2 differ, then explain it back. Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

Boxes and questions

Start Python again and predict each line before pressing Enter:

python3
x = 5
x + 1
x
x = x + 1
x
x == 6
x == 7

x = 5 makes a box called x and puts 5 in it. x + 1 works out an answer but leaves the box alone.

In maths, x = x + 1 is nonsense. In Python, = means “work out the right side, then put it in the box on the left”.

== asks whether two things are equal, and the answer is True or False. One = stores, two == ask. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in programming.

Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

Decisions (20 min session)

Decisions: if

cd ~/course
nvim decide.py

Type this in (i first, Esc and :wq at the end):

n = 7
if n % 2 == 0:
    print(n, "is even")
else:
    print(n, "is odd")

% is the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1. if runs the indented lines under it when its question is True, otherwise the lines under else:. What will it print? Run it:

python3 decide.py

Typos Python can’t see

Make a typo on purpose: in decide.py, change print on line 3 to pirnt, save and run it. Will Python complain? Decide before you read on.

It doesn’t. n is 7, so line 3 never runs, and Python only notices a mistake when it gets there. Now make the same typo on line 5 and run it again: NameError: name 'pirnt' is not defined, with the line number. Fix both with the keys from A shell and an editor: :3, :5, x and i. A program that ran once can still hide a mistake on a line it didn’t reach.

Indentation: what’s inside what

A line ending in : starts a block: the lines under it, indented 4 spaces further. The block ends at the first line that steps back out. nvim indents for you after a :, but it can’t know when a block ends. That’s you, pressing Backspace, and it’s a reasoning question: does this line belong inside?

Copy, then write a recipe (25 min session)

Copy before you change: cp

Your next program grows out of decide.py. Don’t change decide.py itself; copy it:

cp decide.py parity.py
ls

cp copies a file: first what to copy, then the new name. Now there are two, and decide.py still works whatever you do to parity.py. Every program from here on starts as a copy of the last one.

To check your understanding: what would cp parity.py decide.py do? Decide before you read on.

It would copy parity.py over decide.py. cp doesn’t ask: the old decide.py would be gone, with no undo. First name: what you have. Second name: what you’re making.

Recipes: def

nvim parity.py

Change it to this:

def parity(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return "even"
    else:
        return "odd"

print(7, parity(7))
print(10, parity(10))

That’s a lot of changes to a file that already exists. Six more normal-mode keys do it:

Press What it does
dd delete the whole line
O open a new line above, and start typing
o open a new line below, and start typing
>> indent the line 4 spaces
cc retype the whole line (its indent stays)
G jump to the last line

Press Esc after each bit of typing:

  1. On line 1, n = 7: dd.
  2. O, then type def parity(n):.
  3. Down arrow and >>, on each of the four lines under def.
  4. On print(n, "is even"): cc, then type return "even". The same on the other print, with return "odd".
  5. G, o, Enter for a blank line. nvim has indented the new line, guessing it is still inside the recipe. It isn’t: press Backspace once, then type the two print lines.
  6. :wq Enter.

Gone wrong? u undoes. Or :q! and cp decide.py parity.py again: decide.py never changed, so you can always start over.

def makes a function: a recipe with a name, here parity. n is its input: a box that gets a value each time the recipe is used. return hands back the answer and ends the recipe. The recipe is the block indented under def, with the if block inside it.

Writing the recipe down doesn’t run it. parity(7) does: it puts 7 in the box n, runs the recipe and gives back what return hands it. What will the two lines say? Run it:

python3 parity.py

To check your understanding, delete the two print lines and run it again. Why does nothing appear? Decide before you read on.

The file only defines the recipe, and nothing uses it. A recipe on paper cooks nothing. Put the two lines back.

Repeats (20 min session)

Repeats: for

cp parity.py loop.py
nvim loop.py

Replace the two print lines at the bottom with a loop (G, dd twice, then o and type it; nvim indents the line after the : for you):

def parity(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return "even"
    else:
        return "odd"

for k in range(1, 6):
    print(k, k * k, parity(k))

for runs the indented line once for each k in range(1, 6): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. It stops before 6. Work out all five lines, then run it:

python3 loop.py

What exactly does this print?

def parity(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return "even"
    else:
        return "odd"

for k in range(3):
    print(k, parity(k))
    print("done")

How many times does done appear? What changes if print("done") moves one step left, under for? Try both and check.

NoteTry it yourself

Copy loop.py to evens.py and change it to print only the even numbers from 1 to 20. You’ll need an if inside the for, and parity can answer it.

Add 1 to 100 (20 min session)

The story

Around 1785, the story goes, a teacher told his class to add up every number from 1 to 100. A ten-year-old, Carl Friedrich Gauss, wrote the answer almost at once: 5050.

How might he have done it? Spend two minutes with a pencil before reading on.

The slow way: a loop

A new program, so a new file (type it in yourself: typing teaches more than pasting):

cd ~/course
nvim gauss.py
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        print(k, total)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))

sum_to(n) adds up 1 to n: total starts at 0 and the loop adds each k in turn. Work out the first three lines, then run it:

python3 gauss.py

The last two lines say 100 5050, the loop’s last step, and 5050, the answer return handed back to print.

Now make an error on purpose: delete the spaces in front of total = total + k and run it. Read the error, guess what it means, then paste it to Claude with your guess.

ImportantWhy n + 1?

Change range(1, n + 1) to range(1, n). What will the last line be? Run it. An AI makes exactly this kind of mistake, and you just learned to catch it.

Gauss’s trick, checked (25 min session)

Gauss’s trick

Write the sum forwards and backwards:

  1 +  2 +  3 + ... +  99 + 100
100 + 99 + 98 + ... +   2 +   1

Each column adds up to 101, and there are 100 columns. Two copies of the sum make 100 × 101 = 10100, so one copy is 5050. For any :

To check your understanding, explain it to Claude in your own words, without the picture, and let it look for the hole. (Does your explanation work when is odd?)

A check inside the loop

assert means “this must be true here”. Try it in python3, predicting each line first:

python3
assert 4 % 2 == 0
assert 4 % 2 == 1

The first is true, so nothing happens. The second is false, and Python stops with an AssertionError. (Ctrl+D to leave.)

Now put one inside the loop, in a copy of gauss.py:

cp gauss.py invariant.py
nvim invariant.py

Replace print(k, total) with the assert (:5 Enter jumps to it, then cc):

def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))

So this loop checks Gauss’s formula after every step. What should it print? Run it:

python3 invariant.py

It prints 5050: no step failed.

Now break the loop on purpose: change total + k to total + k + 1. At which k will the assert stop it? Then change it back.

A thousand checks, then a proof (25 min session)

Check lots of cases

invariant.py only checks up to 100. sum_to is a recipe, so it can run for any n. Copy invariant.py once more:

cp invariant.py check.py
nvim check.py

Replace the last line, print(sum_to(100)), with a loop over many n (G, cc; after the assert line, Backspace once, so print comes after the loop, not inside it):

def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

for n in range(1000):
    assert 2 * sum_to(n) == n * (n + 1)
print("all 1000 agree")

The recipe is unchanged. The new loop asks, for every n from 0 to 999, whether the loop and the formula agree (twice the sum against , so no dividing). Run it:

python3 check.py

It prints all 1000 agree. Is the formula now true for every number? Decide before you read on.

No. A thousand examples is still just examples. Mathematicians have found patterns that held for millions of cases and then broke.

Why it can never fail

A claim that stays true after every round is a loop invariant, like the assert in invariant.py. Now the big question: if the assert passed in one round, why must it pass in the next? (What does one round add to total?) Decide before you read on.

Say it passed in the round for :

The next round, for , adds , so grows by :
